chunks: Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليهما السلام, who said:
I asked him about the mouse and the dog when they have eaten from the bread or smelled it: may it be eaten? He said: “What they smelled is discarded, and what remains is eaten.”

Then he said—may Allah the Exalted support him: Nothing that dies in water renders it impure except that which has blood of its own. So if a fly, a wasp, a locust, or the like of that which has no flowing blood dies in it, the water does not become impure because of it.

When it has been established by what we have presented from the verse and the reports that waters are, by their ruling, pure, and that their original state is the permissibility of using them, then whatever prevents the permissibility of using them is incidental and requires proof. These things that have no flowing blood—there is nothing in the shari'ah establishing the prohibition of using that into which they have fallen, so it is necessary that it remain upon the original principle. This is also indicated by the previous report from ʿUthmān, from Samāʿah, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, and it is also indicated by it.

key_terms.الطَّهَارَةُ: ritual purity, the original legal state of water
key_terms.الْخُبْزَ: bread, the food item discussed in the ruling
key_terms.الْفَأْرَةِ: the mouse, mentioned regarding contact with bread
key_terms.الْكَلْبِ: the dog, mentioned regarding contact with bread
key_terms.الْمَاءَ: water, the substance whose purity ruling is discussed
key_terms.جَوَازُ اسْتِعْمَالِهَا: the permissibility of using it, the foundational ruling regarding water
key_terms.نَفْسٌ سَائِلَةٌ: flowing blood, the criterion for impurity in this context
key_terms.يُطْرَحُ: is discarded, referring to the affected portion

ai.seo_question: Does a dead insect make water impure, and what is the ruling on bread smelled by a mouse or dog?
ai.summary: This report addresses rulings of ritual purity and impurity concerning food and water. It states that bread smelled by a mouse or dog should have the affected part discarded while the remainder may be eaten, and that water is not rendered impure by creatures that do not possess flowing blood, such as flies and locusts. The accompanying juristic passage affirms the principle that water is originally pure and usable unless a proof establishes otherwise.
